title: Asia stocks fall despite Wall Street records as rising oil, yields weigh
full_text:
Wall Street ends at a record high for the first time since mid-August
Investing.com-- Asian stock markets fell on Wednesday, failing to join an overnight rally on Wall Street that took the S&P 500 and Nasdaq to record highs, as elevated bond yields and renewed gains in oil prices kept investors cautious.
The subdued Asian performance came even as U.S. stocks climbed overnight, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq setting record closing highs. The rally was led by technology and artificial-intelligence stocks.
U.S. stock index futures traded largely unchanged as of 02:55 GMT.
Elevated yields, higher oil drag Asia stocks lower
Japan's Nikkei 225 fell nearly 1%, while the broader TOPIX index edged 0.5% lower.
South Korea's KOSPI declined 1.2%, with heavyweight chipmaker SK Hynix (KS:000660) falling more than 2%. Samsung Electronics (KS:005930) shares dipped 0.6%.
Investors are cautiously awaiting Samsung and SK Hynix's quarterly results later in October, against very high expectations.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng slipped 0.8%, with the Hang Seng TECH sub-index dropping 1.3%.
Mainland Chinese markets remained closed for the National Day holiday, with trading due to resume on Thursday.
Investors remained wary of the bond market. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield remained around 5.3% on Wednesday, while the 30-year yield was above 5.6%, keeping longer-term borrowing costs close to multiyear highs.
Higher yields can reduce the appeal of equities, particularly in emerging markets, while increasing the discount rate applied to future corporate earnings.
Oil prices added to the pressure. Brent crude rose above $101 a barrel and U.S. West Texas Intermediate approached $90 as attacks by Iran-backed Houthi forces in Saudi Arabia heightened concerns about Middle East supplies.
The rise in crude prices revived concerns that higher energy costs could prolong inflation and constrain central banks' ability to ease monetary policy.
RBI rate decision, Fed minutes awaited
Elsewhere, Australia's S&P/ASX 200 traded flat, while Singapore's Straits Times Index traded flat.
Futures tied to India's Nifty 50 fell 0.5%.
Investors awaited the Reserve Bank of India's policy decision later on Wednesday, with the central bank widely expected to raise its repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50%.
The RBI has kept the rate at 5.25% for four consecutive meetings after cutting it by 125 basis points in 2025. Rising oil prices, a weaker rupee and higher global bond yields have intensified inflation risks, with Governor Sanjay Malhotra's comments on the outlook and the policy stance likely to be closely watched.
Investors were also awaiting the minutes of the Federal Reserve's September meeting later on Wednesday, along with speeches from several policymakers.
Markets have sharply reduced expectations for an October rate hike, with the probability of a 25-basis-point increase now around 20%, although an increase in December remains heavily priced.
Investors' focus was increasingly shifting to whether strong corporate earnings can offset the drag from higher energy prices and elevated global borrowing costs.

Investing.com-- Oil prices rose on Wednesday as markets fretted over war-related supply disruptions in the Middle East and U.S. production outages stemming from the Atlantic hurricane season.
Crude extended gains from Tuesday, where increased fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and the Saudi Arabia-backed government in Yemen also spurred fears of supply disruptions, especially after the Houthis claimed to have attacked a major Saudi refinery.
Brent oil futures rose 0.77% to $101.36 a barrel by 21:15 ET (01:15 GMT), while West Texas Intermediate crude futures rose 0.89% to $90.25 a barrel.
Reports of improving oil supplies from the Middle East limited bigger gains in crude, as did planned emergency supply releases by the Group of Seven.

M.East, Gulf of Mexico disruptions in focus
Iran was seen ramping up its pace of attacks in the Strait of Hormuz over the past week– a trend that came just as Gulf producers brought shipments from the region back to prewar levels.
Flows through Hormuz and the Middle East had risen sharply over the past few weeks, coming back in sight of pre-war levels, according to shipping data cited by Reuters. This came as the U.S. continued to offer naval protection against Iran in the region.

The storm is likely to hit offshore oil production in the Gulf, with both Chevron and Shell seen evacuating non-essential personnel from offshore facilities in the region.

U.S. oil inventories fell 2.09 million barrels in the week to October 2, data from the American Petroleum Institute showed late-Tuesday.
The draw comes after three straight weeks of outsized builds, and comes as American producers brace for weather-related disruptions in the Gulf of Mexico.

title: Vance says Iran must reduce nuclear enrichment capacity to end war - Reuters
full_text:

Investing.com-- U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Iran must make a meaningful reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to meet Washington’s demands and end the seven-month war, signaling that concrete nuclear concessions will be central to any diplomatic settlement.

“If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60% enriched fuel?” Vance said, arguing that Iran could demonstrate its commitment to not developing a nuclear weapon by reducing its enrichment capacity.
Iran and the U.S. have exchanged proposals in recent weeks aimed at ending the conflict and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial route for global energy shipments.
President Donald Trump has rejected Tehran’s latest offer and warned that military operations could intensify after the November midterm elections.
Vance said Washington remained open to an agreement but would require concrete action from Tehran.
He also said Washington remained uncertain about who ultimately makes decisions in Tehran, despite talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi.

title: Gold holds gains as oil flows recover, Treasury yields ease
full_text:
Wall Street ends at a record high for the first time since mid-August
Investing.com -- Gold prices held near $4,160 on Wednesday after rising 0.6% in the previous session, as improving oil supplies from the Middle East and a pullback in bond yields reduced pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates this month.
At 20:46 ET (00:46 GMT), XAU/USD fell 0.1% to $4,160.49 an ounce, while Gold Futures rose 0.03% to $4,188.22. XAG/USD was little changed at $61.36, while XPT/USD fell 0.2% to $1,708.06. The U.S. Dollar Index rose 0.1% to 101.95.
Higher Middle East oil flows ease rate concerns
Oil supplies from the Middle East have recovered to roughly four-fifths of pre-conflict levels, according to analysts and research firms, helping ease some concerns over an extended disruption to regional energy flows.
The improvement has helped stabilize oil prices and reduced some pressure on inflation and the Fed's rate outlook.
Still, risks to energy supplies remain elevated.
Iran has increased attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz in recent days, while major oil executives have warned that the industry is running out of temporary measures to manage the disruption as the U.S.-Iran war approaches its eighth month.
Treasury yields also retreated on Tuesday after longer-dated maturities surged to fresh multi-decade highs a day earlier.
The decline in yields has provided some support for gold by reducing the opportunity cost of holding the non-yielding metal.
Fed hike bets fade as gold remains below key averages
Federal Reserve officials have continued to push back against the likelihood of an imminent rate increase.
Traders are now pricing in a less than 20% probability of an October hike, down from about 40% a week earlier.
Minutes from the Fed's September meeting are due later Wednesday.
Policymakers raised borrowing costs at that meeting for the first time in three years, and the minutes could offer fresh clues on the direction of policy.
Gold remains in a relatively tight range in October and is trading below several closely watched price averages.
The metal is also down more than 20% since the U.S.-Iran conflict began in late February, highlighting the sharp reversal from earlier gains.

title: Asian currencies mixed as dollar holds gains, yen weakens near 158
full_text:
Wall Street ends at a record high for the first time since mid-August
Investing.com -- Asian currencies were mixed on Wednesday as the U.S. dollar held near recent highs, while the Japanese yen weakened toward 158 per dollar as markets weighed the Bank of Japan's policy outlook and renewed fiscal concerns.
Higher oil prices and rising Treasury yields kept pressure on the currency complex, while investors awaited the Federal Reserve's September meeting minutes and several Fed speakers for clues on the next rate move.
The U.S. dollar index was around 102.03, up 0.2%, while the USD/JPY pair rose 0.2% to 158.38. The EUR/USD pair fell 0.2% to 1.124, while the GBP/USD pair slipped 0.2% to 1.325. The Australian dollar was around $0.6973 and the New Zealand dollar at $0.5610.
Oil rose as much as 1% to around $101.50 a barrel after Iran increased attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, pushing Treasury yields higher. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield rose three basis points to around 5.31%.
Dollar awaits Fed minutes as hike bets retreat
The dollar has come under some pressure recently after softer U.S. PCE inflation and jobs data reduced expectations for an October rate increase, but markets continue to price further tightening later this year and in 2027.
The chance of a Fed hike of at least 25 basis points in October has fallen to 20.5% from about 51% a week ago, according to CME FedWatch, while markets still price an 84.5% probability of a December increase.
The Fed will release minutes from its September 15-16 meeting later Wednesday, when it raised rates to combat inflation.
Fed officials Christopher Waller, Neel Kashkari and Alberto Musalem are also due to speak. Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid said Tuesday that the central bank still needs to raise rates further to lower inflation.
Yen weakens as BOJ weighs fiscal risks
The USD/JPY pair remained around the mid-158s after a new BOJ board member, Ayano Sato, said she supports raising interest rates in several stages.
The BOJ could signal this month that underlying inflation has broadly reached its 2% target, according to reports citing people familiar with its thinking, highlighting its readiness to raise rates again.
DBS FX & Credit Strategist Chang Wei Liang said the yen could remain slightly weaker as the Japanese government considers a second supplementary budget.
Markets could react negatively because authorities had previously indicated another package was no longer planned and that reserve funds would instead be used for disasters and other emergencies, Chang said.
Rupee in focus ahead of RBI decision
The USD/INR pair rose 0.2% to 96.61, with the rupee under pressure from oil above $100 and higher U.S. yields.
The Reserve Bank of India is widely expected to raise rates by 25 basis points to 5.50%, its first increase since February 2023. Governor Sanjay Malhotra's comments will be closely watched for signals on the subsequent policy path.
DBS Senior Economist Radhika Rao said the macro backdrop has changed materially since the August meeting, with oil prices above $100 and the Fed already restarting its tightening cycle.
Rao said the key question is whether the move is simply a recalibration after last year's rate cuts or the beginning of a longer tightening cycle. DBS expects another hike in the fourth quarter, with the risk of additional increases rising as oil prices remain elevated and weather conditions stay unfavorable.
Across the region, the USD/CNH pair rose 0.05% to 6.7043, while USD/CNY was unchanged at 6.7046. The USD/KRW pair slipped 0.01% to 1,337.85 and the USD/SGD rose 0.12% to 1.2788.
Elsewhere, the euro was pressured by fresh concerns over European fiscal positions. French bond futures underperformed German equivalents as investors assessed the outlook for France's deficit, while Spain's snap-election concerns have added to broader pressure on the euro area.

title: FOMC minutes ahead; Constellation Brands reports - what’s moving markets
full_text:
Wall Street ends at a record high for the first time since mid-August
Investing.com - Futures linked to the main U.S. stock indices inch down, before the release of key minutes from the Federal Reserve’s latest policy gathering. Investors will be hunting for any insight into the Federal Open Market Committee’s policy trajectory, after rate-setters lifted borrowing costs at their September meeting. Elon Musk’s SpaceX reportedly looks to raise $40 billion to purchase more Nvidia chips. Shares of beer producer and marketer Constellation Brands retreat following quarterly earnings, while jeans manufacturer Levi Strauss is due to report.
1. Futures drop
U.S. stock futures pointed lower on Wednesday. By 02:56 ET (06:56 GMT), the Dow futures contract had dropped by 108 points, or 0.2%, S&P 500 futures were mostly unchanged, and Nasdaq 100 futures had dipped by 28 points, or 0.1%.
The main averages on Wall Street crept higher in the prior session, although the indices ended off their earlier highs.
A selloff in U.S. bonds took a breather, while a similar rout in France eased, soothing worries of contagion spreading in global debt markets. But analysts at Vital Knowledge suggested that investors remain skeptical that "this asset class can sustain a material rally," highlighting that a surge in artificial intelligence spending will likely coincide with a "tidal wave" of debt issuance. Benchmark 10-year U.S. and French bond yields moved higher.
Meanwhile, oil prices initially fell, fueling hopes that improving crude shipments out of the Middle East will ease energy-induced inflationary pressures. Yet crude prices eventually rebounded, with reports underlining the massive cost of ferrying oil through the Gulf and an ongoing global shortage of refined products.
2. FOMC minutes ahead
Traders are now looking ahead to the unveiling of minutes from the Fed’s meeting in September, when the central bank raised interest rates for the first time since 2023.
Official projections also hinted at more rate rises to come before the end of the year. Policymakers are keen to corral inflation, which has been hovering well above the Fed’s 2% target for months, due largely to the energy price jump caused by the Iran war.
Still, expectations have faded that the Fed will roll out another rate increase at its next gathering this month. Along with a selection of statements from Fed officials downplaying the urgency of an October hike, recent employment data came in softer than anticipated, likely keeping rate-setters wary of tightening policy so fast that it dents the wider economy.
In theory, raising borrowing costs can put a lid on price gains, albeit at the risk of weighing on the labor market and economic growth.
3. SpaceX to raise $40 billion to buy Nvidia chips - FT
SpaceX is seeking to raise $40 billion in an endeavor led by Apollo Global to buy Nvidia chips, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday, citing people familiar with the matter.
Elon Musk’s rocket and artificial intelligence firm is seeking to raise about $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt for the order, with Apollo expected to lead the deal and help market the debt, the FT report said.
Pimco was among a small group of lenders in talks to fund the deal, the FT reported.
The planned fundraise highlights the large sums that are being poured into data centers, chips, and other infrastructure needed to run AI.
SpaceX is closely tied to Nvidia, with Musk having earlier stated that it would exclusively use Nvidia chips in its Colossus data centers.
4. Constellation Brands slips after earnings
Shares of Constellation Brands fell in after-hours trading, despite the company, whose brands include beers like Corona and Modelo Especial, posting better-than-expected second-quarter profit and sales.
Net sales for the quarter ended on August 31 climbed 6% to $2.63 billion, while earnings per share on an adjusted basis stood at $3.74. Both outpaced Wall Street expectations, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters.
But beer depletions, a critical metric tracking when distributors sell brews to retail accounts, edged down by 0.6%, missing estimates by 70 basis points, analysts at TD Cowen flagged.
They added that management’s decision to reiterate its full-year financial guidance implies that second-half sales "will be down [roughly] 2% at the midpoint." August trends also slowed against a weaker consumer backdrop, likely leading to increased marketing investment in the final six months of the fiscal year, the analysts noted.
Constellation also said it will pay $75 million -- and potentially an additional $278 million over five years -- following the closure of a deal to acquire SpikedAde, a vodka-based ready-to-drink beverage firm.
5. Levi Strauss to report
On the earnings calendar, Levi Strauss is due to report after the closing bell, with the jeans maker banking on the appeal of its premium denim products among wealthier customers despite wider economic uncertainty.
Shares of Levi’s have edged down by more than 1% so far this year, even after the company lifted its full-year profit outlook in July.
Speaking to investors at the time, CEO Michelle Gass said that Levi’s, which has rolled out baggier styles to entice Gen Z shoppers and has focused on building its higher-margin direct-to-consumer business, was attempting to capture a "sizable premium segment" it has not already accessed.

title: RBI hikes rates for first time in nearly 4 years, opens door to more hikes

Investing.com -- The Reserve Bank of India raised its benchmark repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50% on Wednesday, its first rate hike since February 2023, as the central bank responded to a less favorable inflation outlook and heightened geopolitical risks.
The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) increased the policy rate from 5.25%, with the move broadly in line with economists’ expectations. The decision comes as global conditions remain challenging amid geopolitical events, while higher energy prices and other external pressures have complicated the inflation outlook.

RBI turns hawkish, signals scope for further hikes
The rate hike was unanimous, while the MPC voted 4-2 to shift its policy stance from “neutral” to “calibrated tightening,” indicating that most members see room for further increases in borrowing costs.
Governor Sanjay Malhotra said the timing and extent of any additional increases would depend on how inflation and economic growth evolve.
The MPC said the Indian economy is expected to remain resilient, but noted that the inflation environment and its outlook are different from those seen last year.

title: IMF chief warns energy shock, growing debt and AI risks threaten global growth
full_text:
Wall Street ends at a record high for the first time since mid-August
By Rae Wee
SINGAPORE, Oct 7 (Reuters) - The global economy is under threat from persistently high energy prices, record public debt and risks from the AI investment boom, International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Wednesday, urging governments to implement protective fiscal and monetary policy measures.
In a speech previewing IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings next week in Bangkok, Georgieva said the world was being pulled in two directions — a negative energy supply shock from the Middle East conflicts and a positive demand shock from artificial intelligence that is also fuelling inflation.
"The combined impact of these two forces is highly uneven across the world," Georgieva said, adding that the AI boom was bypassing many countries.
New IMF growth forecasts to be released during the Bangkok meetings will show the biggest growth downgrades will come in economies ravaged by war, Georgieva said. These include Ukraine, suffering significant damage to civilian and economic infrastructure, and Gulf countries hit by Iranian strikes and sharply reduced energy exports.
Georgieva did not indicate in her prepared remarks whether the IMF’s latest World Economic Outlook would change the overall 2026 global growth forecast from the sluggish 3.0% rate forecast in July.
That forecast, which predicted a rebound to 3.4% growth in 2027, assumed the Strait of Hormuz would start to reopen in mid-July and return to pre-war conditions by March 2027. It assumed oil prices would average $89 a barrel in 2026 and $78 a barrel in 2027.
Georgieva said oil prices remain at $100 a barrel, with impaired refining capacity adding another $100 in "crack-spread" margins per barrel for key products including diesel. The winter heating season will boost demand even as natural gas supplies remain restricted by threats to LNG shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, she added.
"Even if the war in the Gulf were to end soon, the problem of high energy prices will likely persist for some time," Georgieva said, adding that Brent crude oil futures predict high oil prices through 2027.
Higher energy prices are pushing up inflation, policy rates and benchmark bond yields, she said, noting that US, German and Japanese 10-year sovereign yields are now at their highest levels since 2007, 2009 and 1996, respectively, and still climbing.
GROWING DEBT LOAD
Adding to the worries to be discussed by the IMF’s 191 member countries next week is a growing public debt burden that is sapping growth and adding inflationary pressures, Georgieva said. The IMF says public debt is at the highest level since World War Two and is projected to exceed 100% of GDP before 2030.
Georgieva singled out advanced economies, led by the United States, as the "worst offenders" on debt loads, with debt-to-GDP ratios higher than emerging markets and low income countries.
Policymakers can no longer rely on higher growth rates alone to solve fiscal problems, she said.
"And yet we don’t see decisive action in the high-debt advanced economies where the need of the hour is for credible medium-term fiscal consolidation plans, supported in some cases by upfront fiscal measures, including to take some pressure off monetary policy," she said.
After five-and-a-half years of above-target inflation, Georgieva said inflationary pressures were persisting, from the AI build-out, energy and food price shocks, tariffs, higher defense spending and higher debt service costs.
"Now may be a good time for a prudently hawkish bias in many countries’ monetary policy," Georgieva said, adding that rate hikes by the US Federal Reserve, the ECB and the Bank of Japan were "highly appropriate."
In a fireside chat following her speech, Georgieva added that the "most important task" for monetary policy in the current environment is to focus on price stability and for central banks to communicate their resolve in maintaining it.
"They can only do it when central banks are independent, and when central banks resist pressure that may come from the fiscal side to ease the burden by basically stepping up, buying debt, making it so that the situation from the fiscal side eases," she said.
"I would call this monetary cowboys, running to the rescue of the fiscal agents, and my message is: please don’t."
AI RISKS ABOUND
Georgieva highlighted other risks from AI, where investment as a share of GDP is likely to exceed that of railroads, the electricity grids or telecommunications infrastructure.
The rising economic and financial concentration puts pressure on AI companies to deliver productivity and earnings gains to justify lofty valuations, she said, warning that market disappointment could turn into "a far-reaching shock."
But she said IMF research suggests that AI, done right, could add a half percentage point of extra world growth annually.
AI preparedness is key, she said, including regulatory guardrails that "help manage AI’s substantial perils, which include large-scale labor market fallout, serious cyber and stability risks and frontier models threatening to escape human control and run amok."
In addition to building fiscal strength, even at difficult political costs, Georgieva said governments should take other steps to boost growth, including reforms that would develop improved workforce skills, make corporate startups and wind-downs easier, boost energy security and streamline regulations.

The call, from DA Davidson analyst Gil Luria, rests on a 19x market multiple applied to the firm's FY27 EPS estimate, according to DA Davidson's research note.

The demand logic Luria presents is grounded in how AI models actually consume memory.
"Memory is a lever for better AI performance. AI models generate better results with more memory, run faster with more memory, and have longer context windows with more memory," he wrote.
DA Davidson sees this as a structural shift rather than a cyclical uptick, with the firm asserting that demand will outstrip supply in both 2027 and 2028, a view it says Micron itself validated during its most recent earnings report, where the company guided to both volume gains and price gains through 2028.
One of the more counterintuitive arguments in the note concerns the trend of memory "de-specing" by customers such as Nvidia, which some investors have read as a bearish signal. Luria rejects that interpretation.

In Luria's framing, customers reducing per-unit memory specs to move more product actually creates pent-up demand, because degraded performance pushes them to buy more memory in future product cycles.
He argues that targeting long-term supply contract agreements (SCAs) at roughly 50% of capacity is the right strategic balance, comparing it to airline yield management.

title: UBS says euro zone debt selloff has gone too far
full_text:
Why Barclays says the bull market is "running on tighter margins"
Investing.com --The extra yield that 10-year European Union bonds pay over German Bunds widened to around 59 basis points on Oct. 5 from 39 basis points at the start of September as a selloff in French government bonds spilled over into EU debt, and UBS strategists said the move has gone too far.
In a note dated Wednesday, UBS said EU bonds should keep trading at a premium to Bunds because they are less liquid, but the current gap is "difficult to justify on fundamentals alone."
The strategists said they expect it to narrow partly as market volatility subsides and liquidity conditions normalise.
UBS said the widening reflected renewed demand for Bunds as the euro zone’s only true risk-free asset. It also reflected concern that Ukraine’s future financing needs could lead to more EU borrowing, and uncertainty over negotiations on the 2028-34 MFF.
The strategists said buyers may be focusing more on whether large EU members are willing to back a bigger EU budget and more joint borrowing, at a time when several countries, most notably France, face growing fiscal pressure at home.
UBS said near-term funding risks are limited. The EU’s 2026 borrowing target is unchanged at €180 billion. The bloc raised €99.5 billion in the first half against a revised target of €100 billion, and it plans to issue €80 billion in the second half.
Cash holdings were €121.8 billion at the end of June, almost double the end-2025 level, according to the note. UBS estimated the cash position at around €85 billion to €90 billion as of Oct. 5.
UBS said Ukraine is the main medium-term supply risk. Existing EU programmes appear to cover Ukraine’s 2026 needs, but the International Monetary Fund estimates a financing gap of $30 billion to $35 billion for 2027 alone.
Proposals to seize or directly use frozen Russian assets face significant legal and political obstacles, UBS said. It added that any future shortfall is likely to fall back on EU institutions, raising the probability of additional EU borrowing from 2027.
For 2026, Ukrainian officials estimate a $27 billion defence funding shortfall, of which around $7 billion is expected to be financed domestically, leaving external needs of roughly $20 billion.
The European Commission said on Oct. 2 that €16.6 billion of defence support and a further €17.1 billion of budget support remained available.
Officials at a capital markets seminar held from Sept. 30 to Oct. 1 stressed that while the EU’s NextGenerationEU recovery programme ends in 2026, EU issuance does not, UBS said. It said existing programmes represent around €330 billion of financing needs and imply roughly €50 billion of annual issuance even without new mandates.
The combined debt of the EU, the European Investment Bank and the European Stability Mechanism is expected to approach €1.6 trillion under current mandates and could eventually rise towards €3 trillion to €3.5 trillion, UBS said.
UBS said the EU bond market is also deepening. Secondary-market turnover reached €2.2 trillion in the first half of 2026, almost double the level a year earlier, and average benchmark bond sizes have risen to around €17 billion.
EU-based buyers took 56% of allocations in the first half, UK buyers 27% and Asia-Pacific buyers 9%, according to the note. Bank treasuries’ share rose to 31% from 26% in the second half of 2025, while hedge fund participation almost doubled to around 5%.
Even so, UBS said permanence alone does not make a safe asset. EU bonds still lack a futures contract and the hedging market that supports core government bond markets, it said, and the recent widening suggests market participants still treat them as a spread product, not a safe haven, during stress.

According to recent reporting by The Wall Street Journal, the French government is actively considering boosting its issuance of shorter-term debt as global investors grow increasingly reluctant to lend to the debt-laden nation over longer horizons.
In a recent interview with the Journal, French Finance Minister Roland Lescure noted that the government will need to be "strategic" with its new debt issuance. As a monthslong selloff in French government bonds accelerates, Paris is being forced to adapt to a harsh new reality in the sovereign bond market.
The urgency behind this strategic shift is laid bare by the steep upward trajectory of France’s borrowing costs. Over the past year, the yield on the benchmark 10-year French government bond (OAT) has surged by more than 130 basis points. In early 2026, the 10-year yield was hovering comfortably near 3.2%. By late May, it had climbed past 3.5%, and the selloff accelerated drastically through the fall amid mounting fiscal concerns.
By early October 2026, the 10-year yield spiked to 4.91%—touching levels not seen since 2002—while the 2-year yield climbed to 3.61%. This has dramatically steepened the yield curve, stretching the gap between 2- and 10-year borrowing costs to roughly 1.3 percentage points. Furthermore, the risk premium investors demand to hold French debt over safer German equivalents recently widened to its highest level since the 2011 Eurozone debt crisis. This rapid repricing illustrates exactly why Paris is now looking to the shorter end of the curve for relief.
The bond market is sending a clear signal: investors are demanding significantly higher compensation for the risk of holding French debt over the long run.
"The reasonable thing to do considering the value in the curve, which I see, would lead us to have a shorter maturity," Lescure told the Journal. While he cautioned that this shift would be "at the margin" because governments are "not traders," he admitted that while recent 10-year bond auctions went smoothly, generating demand for 30-year debt is becoming "a bit trickier at the moment."
France is not alone in this pivot. Both the U.K. and the U.S. have shifted toward issuing more short-term debt. The U.S. Treasury has even utilized buybacks of long-term bonds to help suppress yields. However, France has historically relied on longer timeframes; the average maturity of French government debt is currently eight-and-a-half years, compared to just six years for the U.S.
The selloff in French debt is heavily driven by domestic political paralysis. Investors are increasingly concerned that gridlock in Paris is making it impossible for the government to rein in public spending. Despite Lescure’s pledges to force spending cuts through Parliament, markets remain fearful that the country is drifting toward a debt spiral.
Furthermore, analysts point to a structural shift in global demand. Historically reliable buyers of long-term sovereign debt—such as foreign governments and pension funds—are retreating. Without these steady buyers, governments with high debt loads are being forced to adapt to waning demand for longer-term debt.

The creation of a U.S. AI task force and appointment of an AI czar is a positive move because it brings greater certainty for companies and investors, Yabol said, but it should eventually evolve into a fully fledged government agency.
"It brings certainty. It addresses potential risks associated with this new technology," he said, adding that a larger institution would be needed to regulate AI and manage the risks of what he described as a "very powerful technology."
Yabol said governments should first establish clear standards for AI security and risk management before imposing penalties on companies. Regulators currently lack sufficiently clear rules against which AI companies can be assessed, he said.
He warned that rogue behaviour by AI systems could become a major market and security risk if the technology becomes difficult to control. Attempts by AI agents to interact with government systems already show the potential dangers, he said.
If AI systems were to interfere with critical infrastructure such as healthcare or nuclear security, the consequences could be severe for companies and investors, making early monitoring and risk management essential.
Higher rates unlikely to derail AI investment
Higher interest rates could delay some AI investment but are unlikely to stop the broader growth cycle, Yabol said.
If prolonged Middle East tensions keep energy prices and inflation elevated, further rate hikes could pressure capital-intensive AI companies. But investors would continue to fund the sector if expected returns remained attractive relative to bonds and other alternatives.
Yabol also said AI could give developing economies an opportunity to catch up with richer countries by using the technology to accelerate development. The World Bank could eventually help finance infrastructure and safety standards, although major initiatives focused specifically on an AI-based economy have yet to emerge.
The technology could ultimately reshape labour markets and government policy, he said, potentially reducing the availability of jobs and forcing governments to rethink social safety nets.

title: Exclusive-US consumer watchdog examiners adopt lighter touch amid pressure and threats, sources say
full_text:
U.S. stocks fall as Treasury yields resume climb, oil rises; Fed minutes in focus
By Douglas Gillison
WASHINGTON, Oct 7 (Reuters) - Examiners at the US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau gave a largely clean bill of health to most of the companies they inspected earlier this year, a light-touch approach that marked a departure from the past for the watchdog, according to three people with knowledge of the matter.
The CFPB resumed examinations in the spring after President Donald Trump’s administration had suspended most of the agency’s work upon taking office last year.
More than half of those exams went through an "expedited review," which means supervisors identified at most only minor lapses with little risk of harm to consumers, making penalties unlikely, the people said.
Such reviews are more lenient and were historically rare, said the people. But the agency’s new political leadership had made it clear via policy changes and other communications that thorough scrutiny was unwelcome and that examiners’ jobs were at risk, they added.
The high proportion of expedited reviews, which Reuters is reporting for the first time, could expose consumers to harm if the agency overlooked or minimized serious problems, supervisory experts and former agency officials said.
It also shows how the administration’s effort to cut federal workers, narrow exams, and encourage companies to report officials they feel are too tough on them is reshaping frontline oversight of the financial industry, they added.
Representatives for the CFPB did not respond to requests for comment. The White House referred Reuters to the CFPB.
SHIFT IN AGENCY FOCUS
The Trump administration says financial industry oversight has become too onerous, hurting lending and the broader economy, though consumer advocates dispute that. It has also said it is trying to focus examiners on core risks.
Russell Vought, the CFPB’s former acting director, has accused the agency’s staff of "thuggery" in their dealings with firms. He told lawmakers in July that it has shifted its supervisory approach with the aim of doing "as little damage as possible," adding: "That doesn’t mean we’re taking an approach to do... as little as possible."
After initially vowing to abolish the CFPB — which Congress created in the wake of the 2007-2009 global financial crisis — the administration tried to slash two thirds of its workforce, including the vast majority of supervisory staff.
Those plans are now on pause pending confirmation of a new CFPB director.
The agency last year said it would cut the number of exams by half and refocus them away from what had been core areas, such as student loans and medical debt, and more toward mortgages and redress for military service members. It also said it would mostly focus exams on banks rather than nonbanks, such as payday lenders, which the CFPB alone oversees at the federal level.
The agency also now requires examiners to recite a "humility pledge" during exams to work efficiently, transparently and collaboratively with the company concerned. Reuters reported in August that a top CFPB examiner reminded staff of that pledge and warned of "most unpleasant" consequences if they were too aggressive.
Larry Lee, a former CFPB attorney who left the agency in August, said examiners have no incentive to look diligently for violations in the current climate, even as companies benefit long term from robust oversight.
"Today’s undiscovered compliance issues may fester and explode into tomorrow’s widespread but preventable consumer injuries," said Lee, who now leads consumer financial protection policy at nonprofit Better Markets.
EXAMS HELP CATCH PROBLEMS IN REAL TIME
Under the rules, CFPB officials select for examination companies they believe pose the highest risks to consumers, usually after months of analysis.
This year, roughly 70 companies were selected, about half the usual number, with examinations scheduled roughly evenly across four quarters, according to the people and a fourth person with knowledge of the matter. Reuters could not ascertain exactly how many firms were examined in the spring.
Examiners typically inspect records and talk with company employees to uncover any compliance or regulatory violations before deciding how to proceed. In the past, most exams moved to a "full review," involving legal analysis of violations and internal discussions on whether the issue merits enforcement action.
However, this spring examiners in most cases determined the inspections were "clean" under agency guidelines and proceeded with expedited reviews, the three people said. That means they determined that any violations were minor and unlikely to harm consumers, and it was therefore unnecessary to escalate them to legal or enforcement teams, according to public CFPB materials.
Austin Hinkle, former senior counsel in the CFPB’s Supervision Division, said that expedited reviews were traditionally rare because the process was designed to focus on the riskiest companies.
"A significant number of expedited track reviews suggest to me that either political leadership simply picked the wrong companies to examine, or that when violations are identified, career staff are being told to back off," he said.
Examinations are meant in part to correct problems as they are happening. In the past, examiners have identified and swiftly remedied improper vehicle repossessions, harassing or abusive phone calls, attempts to collect money that borrowers do not owe, overcharges and unjustified fees, according to CFPB materials.
Lorelei Salas, who resigned last year as the CFPB’s director of supervision after the agency halted the division’s work, said she felt the CFPB leadership had demonized supervisory staff.
She added that by no longer focusing on nonbanks, it was ignoring "companies that pose the highest risks to consumers" at a time when many are struggling.
"The picture is pretty grim for consumers in the United States," she said.

title: Fed minutes show most policymakers see another rate hike by year end
full_text:
Fed minutes show most policymakers see another rate hike by year end
Investing.com -- Most U.S. policymakers see another interest rate hike by the end of this year, the minutes of the September Federal Reserve monetary policy meeting showed on Wednesday.
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) in that meeting had unanimously raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75%-4.00%, marking the first interest rate hike in over three years. Separately, the Fed’s updated dot plot showed a majority of policymakers anticipating at least one more rate hike this year.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh at the post-decision press conference said the hike would “support a timelier return” to the FOMC’s long-term inflation target of 2%. "The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long," Warsh had told reporters.
"With regard to the outlook for monetary policy beyond the current meeting, most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end," the minutes said.
"Participants emphasized, however, that they approached each meeting with an open mind and decisions at future meetings would depend on incoming information and its implications for the outlook and the balance of risks," they added.
The minutes also showed that all FOMC participants had supported hiking rates in September.
The minutes come at a time when odds of another rate hike by the FOMC later this month have fallen sharply since the September hike, driven by some dovish commentary recently from policymakers and economic data.
Last week, the U.S. personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index ticked up 3.4% Y/Y in August while the core PCE rose 3% Y/Y. Both figures came in lower than anticipated and matched July’s readings. Separately, U.S. Q2 real gross domestic product growth was revised upward to 2.2% from 1.5%.
Later in the week, the September nonfarm payrolls report showed only 29k jobs added in the month, marking the slowest pace of hiring this year.
The indicators together pointed to strong U.S. economic growth, stubbornly high inflation, and some signs of a cooldown in the labor market. Such conditions typically support a central bank keeping interest rates steady, which has been reflected in Fed rate odds. As per the CME FedWatch tool, the probability of the FOMC keeping the target rate steady later this month stood at nearly 81%, down from about 54% a month ago.
"Participants generally emphasized that inflation remained elevated while the labor market appeared to be near full employment, with some signs of strengthening, and that economic activity was expanding at a solid pace. Furthermore, almost all participants assessed that, while inflation risks were tilted to the upside, risks to the labor market had diminished and were now broadly balanced," the minutes said.
"Based on the outlook and the changing balance of risks, all participants viewed a higher target range for the federal funds rate as appropriate. Participants judged that this would support a timelier return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 percent goal," they added.
Fed policymakers had generally sounded hawkish in their public remarks since the September hike, but last week that trend changed after New York Fed President John Williams said there was “no need for urgency” from the Fed to hike rates, adding that there was “time to gather more information.” A day later, Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson also called for careful examination of more economic data before making any future policy moves.
Jefferson also noted that U.S. Treasury yields had soared since the Fed’s September meeting. The benchmark 10-year yield has indeed surged 28 basis points since September 16, in the process hitting its highest levels since early 2002. Yields rise as bonds are dumped, and the increase drives up borrowing costs for U.S. consumers and businesses, effectively acting like a rate hike.
The U.S. bond sell-off has spread to other major markets. The rout has been been driven by concerns around an oil-driven inflationary shock, jitters over the massive amounts of debt being issued by companies to fund their artificial intelligence infrastructure buildouts, expectations of hawkish central bank action, and deepening fiscal issues in countries such as France.
"A few participants discussed the potential factors behind the recent rise in longer-term Treasury yields, such as incoming data that pointed to a stronger economy, increased expectations for AI-related borrowing, and geopolitical developments," Wednesday’s minutes said.
"Many participants commented that, despite the recent rise in longer-term Treasury yields, financial conditions appeared to be supportive of economic growth, with equity prices having risen substantially this year and spreads on corporate bonds having remained narrow," they added.
Wall Street has largely weathered the recent fixed-income ructions, with the benchmark S&P 500 index posting just a 0.5% loss for September and notching a four-session win streak to kick off October, a run that brought the gauge back to record levels on Tuesday for the first time since mid-August. Risk sentiment has benefited from a rebound in the AI trade, expectations of a strong Q3 U.S. earnings season, and the paring in near-term Fed rate hike bets.
The S&P 500 was largely unchanged on Wednesday after the release of the minutes, holding on to slight losses of about 0.2%. The 10-year Treasury yield also did not show much reaction, last up 1.6 basis points to 5.284%.

By Marcela Ayres
BRASILIA, Oct 7 (Reuters) - Brazil presidential candidate Senator Flavio Bolsonaro said on Wednesday his team was studying constitutional amendments to revise parts of a planned consumption-tax reform — alongside other fiscal measures — arguing the current design would leave the country with an excessively high tax burden.
"There are several constitutional amendments that are possible," Bolsonaro told reporters, citing "aspects of the tax reform" among measures he would pursue if elected, alongside lowering the age of criminal responsibility, ending presidential reelection and implementing a political reform.
In 2023, leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva approved the consumption-tax reform, a long-awaited overhaul of Brazil’s tax system, set to begin taking effect next year, which will consolidate multiple levies into a dual value-added tax administered at the federal and regional levels.
"I support modernizing our tax system, which is genuinely too complex," Bolsonaro said.
The reformed consumption tax’s effective VAT rate — estimated to be about 28% by economists but not yet finalized by the government - would be too high, Bolsonaro said.
Bolsonaro also said he wanted to reduce payroll taxes and ensure that "more of Brazilian workers’ income stays with them rather than the government."
On Tuesday, the senator’s top economic adviser, Daniella Marques, told local media that a Bolsonaro administration would review a broad range of tax measures enacted under Lula, including a dividend tax that took effect in January.
Marques served in the elder Bolsonaro’s government. She said that administration had previously only proposed taxing dividends alongside a reduction in corporate income taxes.
Bolsonaro would also eliminate the 12% tax on crude oil exports introduced this year by Lula’s government, Marques said, describing the levy as an "aberration."
Lula introduced the tax to help finance fuel-tax relief for Brazilians amid a global oil-price spike linked to the US-Israeli conflict on Iran.
Other tax measures on the chopping block include reversing increases to the Financial Transactions Tax (IOF) on corporate credit operations, foreign-exchange transactions, and certain private pension investments, Marques said.
By contrast, Lula’s platform pledged to deepen efforts to promote "tax justice" and reduce inequality through the elimination of tax distortions and privileges, while implementing the consumption-tax overhaul approved during his administration.
Lula this year introduced a tax on dividends to help finance an tax exemption on higher income for middle-income earners, while his administration has argued for further cuts to tax exemptions and the elimination of what it views as inefficient tax incentives.
Bolsonaro, the eldest son of ex-President Jair Bolsonaro, outperformed expectations to finish ahead of leftist incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Sunday’s first round. The rivals go head-to-head in an October 25 runoff.
DEBT RESTRUCTURING
Amid near-record levels of household debt in Brazil, Senator Bolsonaro also said his government would buy debt from over-indebted consumers and refinance it through state-owned lender Caixa Economica Federal.
Borrowers would also gain access to new credit lines to help finance small businesses, he said.
Lula, like Bolsonaro, has also pledged to purchase debt as part of a campaign promise.
The government said it will hold an auction in November to buy and restructure household debt, spending 15 billion reais to acquire up to 150 billion reais of delinquent loans at discounts of at least 90%. The program is expected to cover about half of the debt stock deemed eligible.
Households would then be able to clear overdue obligations at the discounted value, with the full benefit of the write-down passed through to borrowers.

By Nandita Bose
SAN ANTONIO, Texas, Oct 7 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump made his third trip to Texas in a month on Wednesday to campaign for Republicans who now face unexpectedly tight midterm election battles as they seek to retain control of Congress.
Trump spoke in a packed arena in San Antonio to support Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, who is locked in a close race with Democrat James Talarico. A loss on November 3 would complicate the party’s path to retaining its slim Senate majority and mark a major setback in a Republican stronghold.
Trump expressed appreciation for Paxton’s loyalty. He endorsed Paxton in the primary after faulting the incumbent Republican senator, John Cornyn, for not supporting him during tough times.
"He was with us all the way," Trump said of Paxton. "He’s a fantastic man and what a job he’s done."
Supporters, some waving cowboy hats, cheered for Trump and shouted "USA," drowning out several protesters who interrupted the event in a Texas city led by a Democrat. Trump said the protesters should "get the hell out of here."
The rally was Trump’s latest effort to mobilize his supporters for Paxton after staging an unusual midterm conventionin Dallas, in part to boost him. But Trump has also publicly criticized his longtime ally, calling Paxton "a pain in the ass sometimes" last week before adding that Republicans "need Ken so badly."
Trump’s repeated trips to Texas are part of a broader push in Republican-leaning states, which were expected to be safely in hand but have instead become midterm battlegrounds. His 32-day campaign blitz has taken him through Texas, Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska, while Vice President JD Vance has campaigned in Alaska. Trump and Vance carried all six states in the 2024 presidential election.
Republicans are struggling as voters focus on high costs and the war with Iran, giving Trump record-low approval ratings. A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed Monday put his approval at 32%, with Democrats leading Republicans 44% to 37% among registered voters.
Trump surprised some Republicans in May by backing Paxton in a party runoff over Cornyn, whom party leaders saw as a safer bet. Republicans are now spending heavily to defend territory they once expected to win comfortably.
Trump won the state by 14 points in 2024, but recent polls have shown Talarico ahead of Paxton. Republicans are also defending competitive House of Representatives seats in South Texas. Both Trump and Paxton attacked Talarico repeatedly in their remarks.
For Trump, the stakes are also personal. James Henson, director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin, said losing the Senate race would be "devastating for Republicans and devastating for Donald Trump" given his support for Paxton. "I think the president clearly will do a lot to try to avoid that outcome," Henson said.
Trump’s political operation has also poured millions into competitive House races. In San Antonio, Republican Carlos De La Cruz, an Air Force veteran, is running in a newly redrawn district, part of a Republican-led remapping that Democrats have called a partisan gerrymander. De La Cruz is expected to speak at Wednesday’s rally.
AN UNEASY ALLIANCE
Trump and Paxton’s relationship has appeared awkward at times. Paxton was recorded telling donors that Republican candidates’ numbers fell after the Trump-centered convention in Dallas, according to the New York Times, while Trump has publicly mocked Paxton’s clothes, speaking style and appearance.
"So to be honest with you, the numbers, when we did that convention, it dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped," Paxton said in the recording. His campaign has disputed suggestions that the remarks amounted to criticism of Trump. A spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.
A New York Time/Siena University poll released October 3 showed Talarico leading Paxton 51% to 45% among likely voters. Brandon Rottinghaus, a political science professor at the University of Houston, said rallying Trump’s base was "necessary but not sufficient" for Paxton.
"Trump’s visits are a catch-22," Rottinghaus said. "The president can inspire as much as he can repel."
Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott, a close Trump ally who is also in a closer-than-expected re-election race, planned to skip Wednesday’s rally, citing other campaign events.
"My rallies are saving the Republican Party, again," Trump said in an all-caps post on Truth Social on Tuesday.
Republicans are betting Trump can still turn out the voters who powered his 2024 victory even as his broader standing has weakened.
The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll showed that just 24% of Hispanic voters approved of his performance. They were an important part of Trump’s success in 2024, when he won nearly half the Hispanic vote, and are a bigger demographic in Texas than most states.

The S&P 500 and tech-heavy Nasdaq slid about 0.2%, a day after both hit record highs.
The pan-European STOXX 600 (STOXX) index ended 1% lower, giving up most of the gains from the last three sessions. Banks took a beating once again, down 3.3%. MSCI’s main world stocks index fell 0.6%.
Oil prices settled lower on Wednesday following a choppy session after the International Energy Agency agreed to speed up a release of oil stocks and prioritize diesel in a bid to curb record-high fuel prices as the Iran war squeezes global supplies. Brent crude futures (LCOc1) settled down 38 cents, or 0.38%, at $100.20 a barrel.
The direction of interest rates also remained in focus.
Minutes released on Wednesday showed Federal Reserve policymakers were divided last month over the rationale for raising interest rates. They showed that "some participants" saw a hike as needed to keep the impact of energy and other price shocks at bay, but a more hawkish core viewed it as necessary to guard against emerging demand-driven inflation.
Russ Brownback, BlackRock’s deputy chief investment officer of global fixed income, said in a note that the latest rate increase did not foretell a predetermined tightening cycle.
"The committee’s decision is more nuanced than a simple conclusion that economic growth is too strong to engender price stability," Brownback wrote. "In other words, the Fed is reinforcing its commitment to be vigilant — not necessarily embarking on a sustained tightening campaign."
US Treasuries rose in afternoon trading on Wednesday, with yields backing away from their highs as oil prices fell and a strong $39 billion auction of 10-year notes reassured investors that demand for long-term government debt remained intact despite recent market volatility.
The yield on benchmark US 10-year notes was last at 5.284%.
